title: SRE standards: SLOs, error budgets, capacity planning, runbooks
author: Ari Chen
body:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning and forecasting, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and canonical runbooks. It is intended as the single source of truth for on-call teams, service owners, and platform engineers.

Goals

- Define measurable SLOs and a clear error budget policy.
- Standardize capacity planning to avoid saturation while optimizing cost.
- Drive continuous reliability improvements through initiatives and game days.
- Provide a consistent incident review process and high-quality runbooks.
- Ensure operational tooling supports rapid detection, mitigation, and post-incident analysis.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

Summary
- SLOs are set at the service/route level and must include an availability (success-rate) SLO and at least one latency SLO where relevant (p95/p99).
- Error budgets are calculated monthly by default. Teams may choose a 30-day or 7-day rolling window for high-churn services with Platform approval.

Naming and ownership
- Each SLO must have: service_name, SLO_name, owner (email), target, window, measurement_query, alerting_policy.
- Example: service: api-gateway; slo: request_success_rate; target: 99.95%; window: 30d; owner: api-platform@redwood.internal

Default SLO targets (guideline; product teams may request exceptions documented in ADR):

Table: Metric | Target | Window
- Availability (global HTTP 5xx + 4xx where applicable) | 99.95% | 30d
- Core latency (in-region p95 for /v1/generate) | <= 250ms | 30d
- Tail latency (p99) | <= 800ms | 30d
- Embeddings throughput (per-request p95) | <= 1200ms | 30d
- Model load success (after deploy) | 99.9% | 7d

Error budget policy
- Error budget = 1 - SLO_target. For 99.95%, monthly budget = 0.05% of total requests.
- Burn rate thresholds and automated actions (per SRE runbook):
  1) Burn rate > 1.0 for 1h: notify owners and on-call, open a ticket.
  2) Burn rate > 3.0 for 30m: trigger immediate mitigation playbooks (scale up, failover) and inform product leadership.
  3) Burn rate > 10.0 for 15m: declare Reliability Incident and engage cross-functional response.

Measurement and tooling
- Canonical SLI measurement lives in monitoring cluster (Prometheus + Cortex queries). Teams must provide the canonical query and a Grafana panel.
- All SLOs are registered in the SLO registry (internal UI). Registration fields: name, target, window, owner, query, dashboards, alert ID.

2) Capacity planning and forecasting

Principles
- Plan for expected growth + 30% buffer for burstability by default. Use historical 90th percentile weekly peak as baseline.
- Distinguish between resource types: GPU inference capacity, CPU workers, disk I/O, and network egress.
- Cost-aware decisions: prefer autoscaling with cold-start mitigations for hosted services; prefer reserved pools for Dedicated tenants.

Process (quarterly cadence)
1) Collect demand signals: API qps, request token distribution, sequence length distribution, model selection mix.
2) Convert to capacity units: use service-specific throughput benchmarks (tokens/sec per GPU type).
3) Run simulation for peak scenarios (1x, 2x, 3x traffic) and failure modes (AZ loss, region outage).
4) Produce capacity plan doc with recommended purchases/reserves, autoscaling params, and rollback thresholds.
5) Review with infra and finance (cost vs. SLA tradeoff) and publish executive summary.

Autoscaling guidelines
- Horizontal autoscaling for model-serving fleets where models are stateless across replicas. Use target CPU/GPU utilization of 60-70% for steady-state.
- For stateful or GPU-backed models with long load times, maintain a warm pool: minimum_reserved_replicas = ceil(expected_peak_qps * safety_factor / replica_throughput).
- Warm pool policy example: maintain 20% extra GPUs during business hours for hosted API; Dedicated customers may configure different policies in their contract.

Capacity runbook checklist
- Forecast inputs attached (traffic, token sizes, model mix).
- Benchmarks used (model_name, GPU type, throughput).
- Scaling tests completed (date and results).
- Purchase orders or cloud quotas requested.

3) Reliability initiatives and continuous improvement

Program elements
- Game days: schedule quarterly cross-team game days targeting high-risk failure modes (AZ outages, cache invalidation, hot-model storms).
- Chaos experiments: controlled fault injection (circuit-breakers, node reboots, high-latency sim). Results go to the reliability backlog.
- Regression monitoring: deploy automated evals against production prompt sets for quality regressions tied to SLOs.
- Runbook drills: monthly runbook walkthroughs with new on-call engineers.

Measure success
- Reduction in incident frequency (target: -20% YoY).
- Mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to mitigate (MTTM) targets: MTTD < 5m for critical alerts; MTTM < 30m for highest-severity incidents.

4) Incident review and postmortem standards

Severity classification (examples)
- Sev 1: Customer-impacting outage affecting multiple customers or core platform (API unavailable globally).
- Sev 2: Degraded performance impacting a subset of customers or increased error rate beyond SLO.
- Sev 3: Low-impact issue, minor customer-facing bug or internal tooling failure.

Postmortem requirements (for Sev1/Sev2)
- Publish a public/internal postmortem within 72 hours. It must include: timeline, impact, root cause analysis (with evidence), contributing factors, action items with owners and due dates, and verification plan.
- Postmortems must follow the blameless format and list systemic fixes prioritized in the reliability backlog.
- Severity escalation and communication: product comms must be notified within the first hour for Sev1.

RCA quality gate
- At least one data-backed root cause (logs, traces, metrics). Avoid single-line root causes without evidence.
- Each action item must be SMART (specific, measurable, assigned, realistic, time-bound).

5) Operational tooling and dashboards

Essential tooling list
- Metrics: Prometheus/Cortex + Grafana dashboards for SLOs, capacity, and model-serving KPIs.
- Tracing: Jaeger/OpenTelemetry instrumentation for request-level traces across the stack.
- Logging: Elastic/Cloud logging with structured fields: request_id, model, tenant_id, sequence_length, route.
- Alerting: PagerDuty for on-call rotation, with escalation policies mapped to severity.
- Incident platform: internal incident tracker with timeline, tasks, and postmortem templates.
- SLO registry UI: central place to browse SLOs, error budget status, and burn-rate history.

Dashboard standards
- Every SLO must have a dashboard tile showing: rolling window availability, error budget remaining, burn-rate graph, and recent alerts.
- Capacity dashboards: cluster utilization, warm-pool size, pending queue length, average and tail latency by model.

Alerting principles
- Alert to action: every alert must have a runbook link and a clear on-call action.
- Avoid alert fatigue: use aggregation and multi-window alerting (short-term spike detection + sustained degradation).
- Use suppression rules during planned maintenance windows and announced deploys.

6) SRE runbooks (canonical templates and examples)

Runbook structure (required)
- Title, service, severity scope, owner, on-call rotation, prerequisites (access, credentials), telemetry & dashboards, step-by-step mitigation steps, escalation path, post-incident actions.

Example runbook: High API 5xx rate (service: api-gateway)
1) Verify: open the API SLO dashboard, confirm increased 5xx rate and affected routes.
2) Identify blast radius: filter by route, tenant_id, and model.
3) Immediate mitigations (choose in order):
   - Rollback recent deploys if deploy timestamp matches start of spike.
   - Scale up frontend and backend replicas by +50% (or follow autoscaler override).
   - Flip to fallback model variant for affected routes (failover policy).
   - Apply rate-limiting at the edge for noisy tenants: request blocking policy with temporary tokens.
4) If mitigations fail in 15 minutes, escalate to on-call infra lead and declare Sev1 if customer impact persists.
5) Capture evidence: collect logs, traces, and heap/gpu stats and upload to incident ticket.
6) Post-incident: open postmortem, include action items, run a runbook drill.

Example runbook: GPU OOM or model crash during inference
1) Check the model-serving dashboard for recent model loads and OOM events.
2) If OOM on a specific model, remove warm pool for that model and redirect traffic to pre-quantized variant.
3) Restart the worker pod and monitor for crash loops.
4) If crash-loop persists, mark the model as degraded in routing (fail closed) and notify model-onboarding team.

Runbook maintenance
- Runbooks must be reviewed quarterly and after any incident that used the runbook. Keep a revision log at the top of the runbook page.
- New on-call members must complete runbook walkthroughs within their first two on-call shifts.
